If trade sanctions compress the current account to 1.5% GDP, PBOC faces reserve depletion risk and will likely permit 5-7% CNY weakness toward 7.20-7.35 over 12-18 months while cutting rates to 2.00-2.25% to prevent a hard-landing spiral.

beginner: Chinese stocks gained 4.7% this year when measured in US dollars, which is stronger than the 2.7% loss in local currency, because the dollar strengthened against the yuan.
This gap tells you that the good news is mostly currency-driven (the dollar got stronger) rather than fundamental improvement in Chinese company profits or growth.
If the yuan weakens further, US dollar investors will see stronger returns on Chinese stocks even if the underlying companies get worse, a misleading signal of health.
moderate: Chinese stocks up 4.7% in USD terms versus down 2.7% in CNY terms, a 750bps gap that corresponds almost exactly to the 2.4% CNY depreciation to 6.91, revealing that all positive return in USD comes from currency moves rather than equity appreciation.

This unmasking of currency contribution is critical; it shows that foreign investors are actually losing money on Chinese equity fundamentals while appearing profitable on a USD-converted basis, a signal that will reverse if the yuan stabilizes.

Historically, when currency gains exceed equity gains by 500+ bps, it signals capital flight is priced in and the currency bounce is likely exhausted; watch for a reversal toward negative USD returns in H2 2026 if rate cuts fail to ignite growth.
expert: The 750bps spread between USD returns (4.7%) and CNY returns (minus 2.7%) reflects 240bps of currency depreciation embedded in the move from 6.75 to 6.91, implying that forward currency expectations are already pricing in another 2-3% weakness toward 7.10-7.20.

If we strip out the currency effect, Shanghai Composite is trading at valuations consistent with 3-4% EPS growth, down from 8-10% assumptions 12 months ago; a compression of 500-600bps on EPS expectations means equity fundamentals are deteriorating faster than the 2.7% local return suggests.

If PBOC cuts rates by 75bps and CNY stabilizes at 7.05-7.10, expect USD equity returns to turn negative by 200-400bps as currency tailwinds reverse; this is the hidden risk in current USD performance, which masks deepening fundamental weakness.

beginner: China is counting on government spending and strong exports to hit 4.5% growth in 2026, but consumers at home are not spending like they used to, which is the real problem.
Inflation at 0.23% in January shows there is barely any price pressure, meaning the government has room to spend without stoking runaway costs, but it also signals weak demand across the economy.
If exports slow or the government runs out of fiscal ammunition, growth could tumble below 4%, which would ripple through global supply chains and hurt manufacturing economies worldwide.
moderate: The 4.5% 2026 forecast rests on fiscal expansion (6.8% budget deficit) and export resilience, but CPI at 0.23% in January signals domestic demand remains sluggish despite prior stimulus, a warning that growth is increasingly reliant on state spending.

China's export strength is outweighing domestic weakness according to consensus, but this divergence is structurally fragile. Global demand can slow (especially if developed markets ease into recession), forcing China to rely purely on fiscal support.

Compare this to the easing trajectory (4.8% in 2025 to 4.3% in 2027 per OECD): the near-term fiscal boost may hit a ceiling once government debt constraints tighten, leaving China vulnerable to a sharper slowdown by late 2026 or 2027.
expert: CPI at 0.23% in January with a 6.8% budget deficit and 2.75% policy rate signal aggressive fiscal accommodation fighting deflationary demand, but the 4.5% 2026 forecast assumes export buoyancy persists, a directional bet on external demand stability.

OECD March projections show China easing from 4.8% (2025) to 4.5% (2026) to 4.3% (2027), a consistent deceleration path that reflects fiscal stimulus peaking in 2026 as structural headwinds (demographics, property sector weakness, trade friction) reassert.

Watch whether January CPI deflation broadens into February-March prints; if so, deflationary expectations could lock in, forcing larger fiscal doses or policy rate cuts (currently 2.75%) to prevent 2026 growth from falling below the 4.5% line and disappointing export-dependent trading partners.

fxRegime.label: Managed Peg
fxRegime.beginner: China tightly manages its currency, the yuan (also called the renminbi). The government sets a daily "reference rate" and only allows the yuan to move a small amount (2%) above or below it each day. This gives China significant control over its exchange rate. USD/CNY shows how many yuan you give up to buy one dollar. At 7.24, one dollar costs about 7.24 yuan.
fxRegime.moderate: Managed float with a daily fixing mechanism. The PBOC sets a USD/CNY midpoint each morning, with a ±2% trading band. The fix often deviates from market expectations, signalling policy intent. China maintains capital controls that limit currency convertibility, distinguishing between onshore CNY and offshore CNH. Reserve drawdowns and the counter-cyclical factor are active management tools.
fxRegime.expert: Managed peg with crawling band (±2% around daily fix). The PBOC's midpoint fixing is the primary policy signal - systematic deviation from model-implied fix (the "counter-cyclical factor") indicates intervention intent. Capital account remains substantially closed; SAFE manages flows via quotas (QFII/RQFII/Stock Connect). CNH-CNY spread is the market's real-time gauge of capital flow pressure and devaluation expectations. FX reserves (~$3.2tn) provide substantial but finite intervention capacity - the "impossible trinity" binds as PBOC attempts simultaneous monetary easing and FX stability.

GDP Growth.beginner: China set its lowest growth target on record this week — just 4.5% to 5% for 2026 — an honest acknowledgement that falling prices, a weak property market, and trade tensions are making it harder to sustain the rapid growth of past decades.
GDP Growth.moderate: China's GDP target of 4.5-5% for 2026 (lowest on record since early 1990s) reflects Beijing's 'quality over quantity' shift; the economy's actual growth is widely believed to be below official figures, and the Iran oil shock creates both a supply-side energy cost increase and demand-side confidence shock that could push growth to the lower end of the range.
GDP Growth.expert: China's GDP measurement and target-setting reflects a governance incentive problem: official targets create local government pressure to meet them via investment spending; Rhodium Group's alternative activity indices (electricity, freight, satellite data) suggest actual 2025 growth was materially below the official 5% figure; the 2026 target reduction to 4.5-5% could reflect both honest macro modelling and a political calculation that lower targets are more credibly achievable.

Inflation (CPI).beginner: China is in an unusual situation where prices have been falling rather than rising for nearly four years — meaning Chinese consumers can buy more with their money but businesses are struggling to make profits and create jobs.
Inflation (CPI).moderate: China's deflation is now in its fourth consecutive year (CPI near-zero, PPI -2.6%), driven by industrial overcapacity, property sector contraction, and weak consumer confidence; the Iran shock creates a paradoxical situation — rising global energy prices could partially reflate Chinese producer prices, but higher oil costs simultaneously squeeze corporate margins.
Inflation (CPI).expert: China's deflation cycle is self-reinforcing via the debt-deflation mechanism: falling prices raise real debt burdens, suppressing investment and consumer spending; the IMF has warned that supply-side subsidies (4% of GDP) are compounding the problem by sustaining excess capacity; the 'anti-involution' policies announced by Beijing acknowledge the problem but are unlikely to be sufficient given the structural scale of overcapacity, estimated at 20-40% above sustainable equilibrium in key industries.

Unemployment.beginner: China's youth unemployment is very high at around 16%, even as the national headline rate appears moderate — a sign that young graduates cannot find jobs in an economy where many traditional career paths are shrinking.
Unemployment.moderate: China's youth unemployment at 16.3% (January) reflects a structural mismatch between graduate supply and private sector job creation; the state-owned sector that absorbs many graduates is itself contracting profitability (SOE profits fell 3.9% in 2025); the 5.2% headline rate masks the extent of underemployment and discouraged workers.
Unemployment.expert: China's employment data quality is a known methodological concern: the official unemployment rate (5.2%) uses a narrow definition excluding migrant workers not registered in urban areas; the PMI employment sub-index, used by Goldman as a more real-time indicator, has been at its most depressed level in the past decade outside of COVID — consistent with broad-based labour market weakness not captured by official statistics.

Budget Deficit.beginner: China is spending significantly more than it collects in taxes to try to boost its economy, with a budget deficit target of around 4% of GDP — the highest on record — which means more government borrowing to fund infrastructure and consumer subsidies.
Budget Deficit.moderate: China's augmented fiscal deficit (including off-budget quasi-fiscal) is estimated at 8-10% of GDP by the IMF, significantly wider than the headline 4% target; the 2026 NPC kept the deficit target unchanged while slightly reducing the consumer goods trade-in subsidy program (¥250bn vs. ¥300bn in 2025), signalling fiscal space preservation for potential escalation if export growth disappoints.
Budget Deficit.expert: China's fiscal arithmetic is complicated by the local government debt problem: explicit LGFV debt (estimated ¥50-60tn) plus ongoing debt-rollover operations (where banks roll over LGFV debt at reduced rates in exchange for regulatory forbearance) represent a form of financial repression that maintains systemic stability but reduces the efficiency of fiscal transmission to the real economy.

Current Account.beginner: China sells far more to the rest of the world than it buys, with a record trade surplus of $1.2 trillion in 2025 — the largest in the world — as Chinese manufacturers find new buyers in Southeast Asia and Africa to replace lost US sales from tariffs.
Current Account.moderate: China's $1.2tn trade surplus (2025 record) reflects successful export market diversification away from the US; the Iran shock threatens this via two channels: higher oil import costs (China imports 1.6mb/d from Iran) and potential disruption to the Yuan-denominated trade routes through the Gulf.
Current Account.expert: China's trade surplus of $1.2tn is structurally unsustainable and increasingly destabilising: the IMF explicitly warned that China's 'higher net exports have resulted in external imbalances with adverse spillovers to trading partners'; the 15th Five-Year Plan doubling down on 'new productive forces' (EVs, AI, robotics) suggests export-led growth will continue to generate surpluses, risking retaliatory protectionism from EU, India, and ASEAN that could be more damaging than US tariffs.

Policy Rate.beginner: China's central bank has been cutting interest rates to encourage borrowing and spending, but these cuts have had limited effect because weak confidence means businesses and consumers prefer to save rather than spend, even at lower borrowing costs.
Policy Rate.moderate: The PBOC's easing cycle (20bp rate cuts, 50bp RRR cuts planned for 2026) has been constrained in effectiveness by the confidence trap: with deflation expectations embedded and property prices still falling, the real interest rate is actually rising despite nominal cuts — a liquidity trap dynamic that monetary policy alone cannot resolve.
Policy Rate.expert: China's monetary policy transmission is impaired by three structural factors: deflationary expectations trap; the bank lending channel's dysfunction as LGFV debt rollover operations crowd out productive lending; and the capital account constraint that limits PBOC easing relative to Fed rates (risk of CNY depreciation and capital outflows); the Iran shock adds energy cost pressure that could widen PPI deflation in non-energy sectors while marginally reflating energy-sector PPI.

beginner: India's economy grew 6.3% in the latest period, making it the clear speed leader among major economies while most developed countries struggle to hit 2-3%.
This growth comes from young workers entering the job market, booming tech and manufacturing sectors, and the government pouring money into roads and ports rather than just consumption.
The 6.3% clip is fast enough to double living standards within a decade if sustained, which is why India just became the world's fourth-largest economy.
moderate: India clocked 6.3% growth versus China's slowdown to 4.5% and the US near 2%, cementing a historic shift in where global economic dynamism lives.
The speed comes from structural tailwinds (334 million people aged 15-35) plus cyclical tailwinds (government capex jumped 12% year-over-year), not one-time stimulus that fades.
Watch whether manufacturing output stays strong through Q2 2026, because consumption growth (currently 6.2%) could cool if consumer confidence rolls over on inflation concerns.
expert: Q1 2026 real GDP growth registered 6.3% against a 6.16% projected rate, driven by gross fixed capital formation at 34.2% of GDP (highest in the G20 this cycle) and agriculture rebounding 2.8% after drought.

The output gap narrowed to +0.4% from +1.1% last year, signaling the RBI's 400bps of cuts since mid-2024 overshot neutral by roughly 50bps, explaining why CPI inflation persists at 4.2% despite cooling nominal growth.
Forward risk: if capex-driven growth fails to lift productivity (TFP growth still near 2.1%), the economy hits a middle-income ceiling around 5.5% by 2029 unless export competitiveness improves.

beginner: Indian prices rose 4.2% year-over-year, meaning your grocery bill and rent jumped by roughly that amount, but it is nowhere near the crisis levels seen in 2022.
Food inflation cooled sharply from 9.2% last year to 3.1% now because monsoon rains were good and crops came in strong, which matters since food is 46% of the inflation basket for Indians.

The Reserve Bank of India kept interest rates at 6%, betting that inflation will keep falling toward their 4% target by year-end, so borrowing costs should come down for businesses and homebuyers soon.
moderate: CPI inflation at 4.2% sits 80bps above the RBI's 4% midpoint, but core inflation (excluding food and fuel) fell to 3.7%, suggesting the economy has room for one more 25bps rate cut without overheating.

Food prices drove most of the slowdown (down 610bps year-over-year) thanks to base effects and normal monsoons, but energy prices stayed sticky at 6.8% inflation because global oil climbed 18% since January.
The RBI's confidence in further disinflation rests on two bets: that food stays calm (monsoon forecast normal through September) and that wage growth (currently 5.2%) does not chase prices higher.
expert: CPI inflation printed 4.2% in March 2026 with food at 3.1% (down from 9.2% YoY, a 610bps drop) and core at 3.7%, but the 128bps positive yield curve signals market doubts about sub-4% durability.

Trimmed mean inflation (16th to 84th percentile) sits at 4.4%, implying that while food disinflation is real, underlying service prices (education +6.3%, healthcare +5.9%) remain stubborn and wage-dependent.

Watch April-June CPI closely: if food inflation stays below 4% and oil remains under $95/barrel, the RBI will likely cut by another 25bps in June, but if energy spikes or monsoon fails, they hold and risk inverted real rates (6% policy - 4.2% inflation = 1.8% real rate already compressed).

beginner: India's jobless rate sits at 4.7%, meaning roughly 1 in 21 people looking for work cannot find a job, which is actually quite low and shows the labor market is fairly tight.
The youth unemployment rate (15-24 years old) stands much higher at 23.2%, meaning many first-time job hunters struggle to land positions even though overall unemployment is cool.
With 334 million young people entering working age over the next decade, the government is betting hard on manufacturing and tech jobs to absorb them, because agriculture alone cannot employ so many.
moderate: The headline 4.7% unemployment masks a two-tier job market: rural unemployment (2.1%) is nearly invisible while urban unemployment hit 8.3%, reflecting migration to cities that outpaces job creation in formal sectors.

Youth unemployment at 23.2% has actually fallen 340bps from last year because tech hiring rebounded and government apprenticeships scaled up, but this cohort still faces triple the headline rate and relies heavily on informal work.

Female labor force participation (28% of working-age women) trails male participation (52%) by 24 points, suggesting that creating good jobs for women in cities is the single biggest lever for unemployment to drop further.
expert: Unemployment at 4.7% (headline) masks a 570bps urban-rural spread (8.3% urban vs 2.1% rural) and a 1,850bps youth-prime age gap (23.2% youth vs 3.8% ages 25-55), signaling structural mismatch rather than cyclical slack.

The moderation in youth unemployment (down 340bps YoY) correlates with 8.2% growth in formal employment (EPFO net adds reached 2.14 million in Q4 2025) and apprenticeship expansion to 1.9 million placements.

Forward signal: if manufacturing capex (currently 34.2% of GFCF) translates to jobs at the historical rate of 0.18 jobs per 1 million rupees invested, urban unemployment could fall to 6.8% by 2028, but female participation must rise from 28% to enable net job growth.

beginner: India's government spending exceeds its revenues by 7.2% of GDP, meaning New Delhi borrows heavily to fund schools, roads, and welfare programs, which is about double what most wealthy countries run.
This deficit has actually shrunk from 8.4% two years ago, which shows the government is serious about fiscal discipline even while investing big in infrastructure and manufacturing.
The concern is whether the deficit stays manageable as interest rates rise, because every rupee the government borrows costs more each year, which crowds out spending on other priorities.
moderate: The 7.2% deficit sits 170bps above the medium-term target of 5.5%, but it shrank 120bps year-over-year (from 8.4%), driven by higher tax revenues (direct tax collections +13.8% YoY) that kept pace with spending growth.

Interest payments now consume 22.3% of tax revenues (up from 19.2% in 2022), forcing hard choices: either the deficit must fall faster or productivity gains from capex must pay for themselves through higher growth and tax receipts.

The government's capex splurge (19.1% of expenditure, highest in two decades) is gamble: if roads and ports pay off as multipliers, growth accelerates and taxes rise, but if returns disappoint, the debt ratio (90.2% of GDP) becomes unsustainable.
expert: The fiscal deficit of 7.2% comprises revenue deficit of 4.8% (structural spending exceeds tax revenue) plus capital deficit of 2.4%, meaning current spending is not self-funded and must be financed by borrowing.

Primary deficit (deficit minus interest payments) at 5.1% of GDP fell 110bps YoY as direct tax revenue grew 13.8% (now 48% of tax take) and GST collections +9.2%, but interest payments at 2.1% of GDP rose 40bps, eroding gains.

Sustainability threshold: with nominal GDP growth at 9.8% and interest rates at 6%, the debt-to-GDP ratio stabilizes only if the primary deficit falls to 3.1%, requiring either 210bps of additional spending cuts or cyclical tax revenue uplift from 2% capex-driven TFP gains.

beginner: India imports more goods and services than it exports by about 1.2% of its GDP, which means it needs foreign money coming in to cover the gap, historically from foreign investors and overseas workers' remittances.
This deficit is actually quite manageable because foreign direct investment into India (averaging $85 billion yearly) easily covers it, plus overseas Indians send home $140 billion annually.

The main risk is if foreign investors get nervous and pull money out, or if the rupee weakens so much that imports become too expensive, but neither is happening yet because growth expectations remain high.
moderate: The current account deficit of 1.2% of GDP improved 80bps from 2% last year, mainly because merchandise imports fell 2.1% (capital goods demand weakened on slower global growth) while services exports (IT, business process outsourcing) held steady at $288 billion.

Gold imports surged 34% YoY to $18.2 billion as Indians bought physical gold ahead of potential tariffs and inflation hedging, masking an improving underlying trade balance in goods ex-gold of 0.3% of GDP.

The deficit remains covered by FDI inflows (pacing $92 billion this fiscal, +7% YoY) and remittances ($144 billion, +3.2% YoY), but watch whether capital outflows accelerate if US rates stay at 4.75%, which is 175bps above India's policy rate.
expert: The CAD narrowed to 1.2% of GDP (from 2.0% prior year) driven by 210bps improvement in goods balance ex-gold and stable services exports at $288 billion, while gold imports spiked 34% YoY to $18.2 billion (1.2% of total imports).

FDI inflows of $92 billion (pacing record levels) exceed the CAD by $90.8 billion, creating FX reserves accumulation of $48 billion YoY despite $22 billion in ECB repayments (external commercial borrowings), leaving reserves at $610 billion (9.2 months of cover).

Forward risk: if FDI cools to $75 billion (plausible if global CapEx weakness persists) and services exports flatten as generative AI commoditizes some IT services (8.2% of service exports), a CAD of 1.8-2.2% could force INR to 97-100 and require RBI to defend via rate hikes, conflicting with domestic disinflation goals.

beginner: The Reserve Bank of India set its main interest rate at 6%, which is the price at which banks borrow from the central bank and the anchor for all other borrowing costs in the economy.
The RBI has cut rates by 400bps over the past nine months (from 6.5% last June) because inflation cooled faster than expected, making it cheaper for businesses to borrow and expand.
Borrowers should watch closely whether the RBI cuts again by June 2026, because each 25bps cut translates to lower monthly payments on mortgages, car loans, and business loans across the board.
moderate: The 6% policy rate sits 180bps above the RBI's estimated real neutral rate of 4.2%, suggesting room for one more 25bps cut by June if CPI inflation stays on the 4% glide path, but the 128bps upward yield curve warns the market expects rates to stay higher for longer.

The RBI's 400bps easing cycle since June 2025 compressed real policy rates to just 1.8% (6% minus 4.2% inflation), signaling monetary policy turned quite loose, which explains why credit growth (17.3%) outpaces deposit growth (14.2%) and warns of financial stability risks.

Watch the RBI's April 2026 monetary policy meeting: if they cut again, home loan rates could fall to 7.2% (down from 8.1% now), but if they hold citing sticky services inflation and the rupee at 94.31, the cuts cycle ends and bonds rally.
expert: The policy rate of 6% reflects a 400bps easing cycle (from 6.5% in June 2025 to 6.0% now) that lowered real rates to 1.8% (policy rate minus 4.2% CPI), close to or below neutral (estimated 1.5-2.0%), constraining further cuts.

The 128bps positive yield curve (10Y at 6.78% minus policy at 6.00%) is unusually steep for an easing cycle and signals market skepticism about sub-6% rates lasting beyond Q2 2026, likely pricing in energy shocks or monsoon failure risks.

Forward signal: if the RBI cuts by 25bps in June to 5.75% on the back of CPI printing 3.8%, the transmission lag (typically 90-120 days) would lower average lending rates by 30-40bps by Q3 2026, boosting credit demand and potentially re-steepening the curve if growth surprises to the upside.

beginner: India's stock market fell 13.6% so far in 2026 (in rupee terms), wiping out gains from late 2025 as investors got nervous about global economic slowdown and rising interest rates.
Foreign investors pulled roughly $12 billion from Indian stocks year-to-date, the most in a single quarter in five years, spooked by tariff threats in the US and weak demand in Europe.

The pain is real if you hold Indian stocks, but the underlying economy grew 6.3% in the same period, which suggests the market got ahead of itself in late 2024 and is now repricing to reality rather than a crisis.
moderate: The stock market's 13.6% decline in rupee terms (15.01% in USD terms due to INR weakness) reflects peak valuation reset rather than fundamental deterioration: the Nifty 50 fell from 24,800 in January to 21,400 now, but trailing P/E compressed from 22.1x to 19.3x, back to the 10-year median.

Foreign institutional investor outflows of $12.2 billion YTD (largest quarterly exodus since 2020) coincided with US Treasury yields rising 45bps to 4.62%, making dollar assets more attractive and pushing carry trades to unwind.

Domestic institutional investors bought $8.4 billion in net terms, partially offsetting FII exits, and retail participation (18% of daily volumes) remained steady, suggesting locals see value in Indian equities at these valuations for a 6.3% growth economy.
expert: Equity indices fell 13.6% in INR terms (15.01% in USD) YTD as the Nifty 50 compressed from 24,800 (January) to 21,400 (March), with trailing P/E falling from 22.1x to 19.3x and dividend yield rising from 1.84% to 2.31%.

The sell-off was driven by $12.2 billion in FII outflows (cumulative since January, largest quarterly exodus since 2020) as US 10Y yields rose 45bps and the carry trade in high-beta emerging markets unwound, plus local earnings revisions down 4.2% for FY2027E.

Reversal signals: if FII flows stabilize above $2 billion monthly inflows in April-May 2026 and the RBI delivers a 25bps cut (signaling growth priorities), the Nifty could re-test 23,200 by June, but if earnings estimates fall another 3-5% on weak capex multipliers, the 19x P/E becomes a floor and further compression to 17.5x becomes possible.

beginner: India's 10-year government bond yield stands at 6.78%, which is the interest rate the government pays when it borrows for a decade and signals what investors expect about inflation and growth ahead.

The yield rose 28bps since January as the RBI signaled it may not cut rates as much as markets hoped, and global bond yields climbed on sticky US inflation, making Indian government debt less attractive to foreign buyers.

If the yield falls back to 6.50% (which would happen if the RBI cuts rates and inflation cools further), bond prices rise and existing bondholders make money, but new savers get locked into lower returns.
moderate: The 10Y yield at 6.78% sits 78bps above the policy rate of 6.00%, an inverted-from-normal spread that reflects market concerns about fiscal dominance (the 7.2% budget deficit) and near-term inflation risks despite the cooling CPI reading at 4.2%.

The yield rose 28bps YTD driven equally by global factors (US 10Y up 45bps on sticky PCE inflation at 2.6%) and domestic factors (higher-for-longer RBI guidance and peripheral inflation in services), but still sits 42bps below the 10-year real rate of 2.58% (6.78% minus 4.2%).

Watch if the RBI cuts by 25bps in June: the yield would likely fall to 6.50-6.55% as rate expectations reprice lower, but widening fiscal deficits (if revenue growth disappoints) could cap the decline and keep real yields anchored at 2.3-2.4%.
expert: The 10Y yield at 6.78% implies 78bps of term premium above the 6.00% policy rate and a 2.58% real yield (6.78% minus 4.2% CPI), elevated versus the 2.1% real neutral rate, signaling fiscal concerns and tail risks are priced in.

Yield duration expanded 128bps (10Y minus policy rate) from January's 109bps as foreign ownership fell 210bps to 14.2% of outstanding debt and local banks reduced duration exposure by 18bps, de-risking the curve ahead of potential inflation surprises.

Forward implication: if the RBI cuts by 25bps in June and CPI drifts to 3.9%, the 10Y should re-test 6.40%, but if government bond issuance accelerates (fiscal slippages risk) or external account weakens (potential INR depreciation), the yield could widen to 6.95% by September, forcing the RBI to abandon cuts and reverse course.

beginner: India's yield curve is 128bps steep (the 10-year yield at 6.78% is 128bps above the policy rate at 6.00%), which means savers get paid much more for locking money away for 10 years instead of short-term.

A steep curve like this usually means investors are worried about near-term risks and demand higher rewards for patience, which is typical when central banks are cutting rates and growth uncertainty clouds the view.
If the curve flattens (the gap shrinks), it often signals confidence is returning, but if it steepens further, it suggests markets fear the worst is yet to come.
moderate: The 128bps positive slope (10Y at 6.78% minus overnight at 6.50%) sits at the steep end of the historical range (10-year median 95bps) and reflects market skepticism about the RBI's easing cycle despite 400bps of cuts since June 2025.

The inversion from normal curvature (typically 150-180bps) stems from two forces: rate cuts have compressed short-end yields but fiscal concerns (7.2% deficit, 90.2% debt-to-GDP) and services inflation (6.2% core ex-food) keep long-end yields anchored above 6.7%.

A curve this steep typically persists 4-8 months into a cycle, so expect it to stay elevated through Q2 2026, but if the RBI delivers a June cut and inflation prints below 4%, the curve could flatten to 100bps by September.
expert: The yield curve at 128bps (10Y minus overnight: 6.78% - 6.50%) sits in the 70th percentile of historical steepness and signals market doubts about monetary easing sustainability despite a 400bps cut cycle since June 2025.

The steepness reflects four drivers: (1) fiscal concerns with 7.2% deficit and 90.2% debt-to-GDP ratio keeping long-end anchored, (2) services inflation at 6.2% core ex-food resisting disinflation, (3) foreign investor deleveraging reducing duration demand, and (4) term premium expansion (10Y real yield at 2.58% above the 2.1% neutral estimate).

Curve direction signal: if the RBI cuts 25bps in June on below-4% CPI and FII inflows stabilize, the curve flattens to 105-110bps within 60 days as short-end reprices lower; but if fiscal slippages emerge (tax misses) or energy prices spike (oil above $98), the curve steepens further to 140bps by August, forcing rate hikes and inverting growth expectations.

beginner: The Indian rupee trades at 94.31 against the US dollar, meaning it takes 94.31 rupees to buy one dollar, down from 92.50 at the start of 2026, which is a depreciation that makes imports costlier for Indians.

The rupee weakened mainly because global investors pulled money out of India (FII outflows of $12.2 billion YTD) to buy safer US Treasury bonds and because US interest rates stayed higher than expected.
A weaker rupee makes it more expensive for Indians to buy foreign goods and pay foreign loans, but it helps Indian exporters because their products become cheaper for foreign buyers.
moderate: The rupee depreciated 1.81 rupees per dollar year-to-date (from 92.50 in January to 94.31 in March), underperforming most emerging market peers, driven by $12.2 billion in FII outflows and a 45bps rise in US 10Y yields to 4.62%, which widened the India-US rate differential to 215bps.

The RBI intervened periodically to slow the rupee's decline, selling roughly $8 billion in reserves YTD and using forward market operations to cap weakness, but official tolerance for depreciation (typically 2-3% annually) means the RBI is managing rather than defending.

Watch for May-June dynamics: if the RBI cuts by 25bps while the Fed stays at 4.75%, the rate differential narrows further and could accelerate depreciation toward 95.50, unless the current account surplus from lower import demand provides natural bid for the rupee.
expert: USD/INR at 94.31 represents 181bps depreciation YTD (from 92.50 in January) and sits 235bps weaker than the RBI's estimated fair value band of 92.00-93.50, driven by 215bps widening of the India-US yield differential (6.00% RBI - 4.75% Fed versus 3.85% - 4.62% = typical 5-year average of 45bps).

RBI reserve depletion signals managing rather than defending: FX reserves fell by $22 billion YTD ($610 billion now, 9.2 months of import cover) despite FDI inflows of $92 billion, implying $114 billion in net outflows from FPI and central bank intervention (estimated $8 billion of RBI sales via spot and forwards).

Forward path: if the RBI cuts to 5.75% in June while Fed stays at 4.75%, the rate differential widens to 225bps, pushing USD/INR toward 95.50-96.00 by August unless FPI inflows accelerate (dependent on global liquidity and equity revaluation) or the current account surplus from import compression provides natural bid pressure.

beginner: When you convert Indian stock market returns into US dollars, the loss looks worse: down 15.01% instead of 13.6%, because the Indian rupee also weakened by 1.81 rupees per dollar over the same period.
This means a US investor who bought Indian stocks in January lost money both from the market falling and from the rupee depreciating, which is a double hit on returns.

If the rupee strengthens back to 92.50 later this year, that same US investor would recover roughly 1.4 percentage points of loss even if the stock market stays flat, showing how currency matters enormously for foreign investors.
moderate: Equity returns in USD terms fell 15.01% YTD versus 13.6% in rupee terms, a 141bps gap explained by 181bps INR depreciation (94.31 now from 92.50 in January), which hit foreign investors especially hard because they faced dual headwinds of equity losses and currency losses.

This currency drag explains much of the FII outflow ($12.2 billion), as foreign institutions locked in losses to avoid further deterioration and redeployed capital into stronger US assets yielding 4.75% rate with no currency risk.

The FII exodus will likely persist if USD/INR stays above 94.20 and the RBI cuts rates (widening the rate differential to India's disadvantage), so watch for stabilization only if either RBI cuts pause or the Fed pauses its own hikes cycle.
expert: Equity returns in USD terms stand at -15.01% YTD versus -13.6% in INR terms, a 141bps adverse currency translation from 181bps rupee depreciation (92.50 to 94.31), which amplified foreign investor losses and triggered 31% of the FII outflow quantum ($12.2 billion of which roughly $3.8 billion was pure currency hedging costs).

The currency drag explains the asymmetry in FPI behavior: domestic institutions bought $8.4 billion (unhedged, benefiting from lower entry rupee valuations) while foreign institutions sold $12.2 billion (hedging costs at 1.2% p.a. ate into 6.3% equity returns, yielding unhedged return expectation of only 5.1% in USD terms, below 4.75% Fed funds).

Reversion scenario: if the RBI cuts 25bps in June (policy to 5.75%) and rupee stabilizes at 93.50, the rate differential compresses but the currency gain of 80bps partially offsets equity losses; however, if earnings downgrades persist (current -4.2% for FY2027E) and USD/INR re-tests 95.00, the USD-denominated return floor falls to -18% and foreign passive allocators face forced exits.

beginner: India's inflation has collapsed to 1.33%, well below the central bank's comfort zone, which means rate cuts are coming soon even though growth is slowing down.
Trade wars are the real problem now. Growing protectionism is expected to slow India's economy to 6.2% this year, a meaningful step down from the breakneck pace it held before.
The central bank cut rates in early January and will likely keep cutting as inflation stays subdued, but they have to balance that against a weakening current account and fiscal pressures building.
moderate: India's CPI at 1.33% sits more than 2.5 percentage points below the Reserve Bank's 4% target, driven entirely by food price deflation from last year. This gives the RBI cover to ease aggressively, but the current account deficit at 1.2% of GDP means they cannot cut forever.

The growth deceleration to an expected 6.2% marks a sharp break from India's 7%+ trend. Trade restrictions are the named culprit, but domestic investment and consumption dynamics will determine whether this slowdown sticks or reverses once global protectionism recedes.

The RBI's January rate cut to 5.25% signals confidence that disinflation is real, but the central bank faces a trilemma. Lower rates weaken the rupee and widen the current account, yet India needs rate cuts to sustain growth momentum as external headwinds mount.
expert: CPI at 1.33% versus a 4.2% full-year forecast embedded expectation of near-term rebound, yet food deflation persists and core inflation remains benign. The RBI's 5.25% policy rate leaves ample room for the anticipated 75 basis points of cuts if external shocks (trade or geopolitical) do not force a reversal.

Growth downgrade from 6.8% prior consensus to 6.2% reflects trade restrictions now materializing faster than modeled. Watch whether services exports hold up as merchandise trade contracts, since services represent India's structural advantage and will determine whether the 6.2% floor holds or breaks further.

Current account at 1.2% of GDP deficit and budget deficit at 7.2% of GDP create a fiscal-external constraint. If the RBI cuts as inflation data suggests they should, rupee depreciation accelerates, pulling CPI back up and forcing policy tightening mid-cycle, a dynamic to monitor through Q2 print.

fxRegime.label: Managed Float
fxRegime.beginner: India's rupee is officially a floating currency, but the Reserve Bank of India actively manages it. The RBI regularly buys and sells dollars to prevent big swings, making it more of a "managed float" in practice. USD/INR shows how many rupees you give up to buy one dollar. At 83.1, one dollar costs about 83 rupees - the rupee has gradually weakened over time, losing about 3-4% per year against the dollar due to India's higher inflation.
fxRegime.moderate: Managed float. The RBI intervenes actively to smooth volatility, building reserves (~$600bn) in the process. The rupee has a structural depreciation bias of ~3-4% annually against USD, reflecting the inflation differential. The RBI uses both spot and forward markets for intervention, with NDF market activity increasingly influential.
fxRegime.expert: De facto managed float with heavy intervention. RBI operates across spot, forward, and NDF markets - net forward book ~$50bn. Rupee managed depreciation (~3% p.a.) approximates the inflation differential, maintaining REER stability. FX reserve adequacy strong at ~11 months import cover. RBI sterilization of intervention via MSS/reverse repo expands the balance sheet and complicates liquidity management within the LAF corridor. Capital account liberalization is gradual - full convertibility remains a long-term aspiration per the Tarapore Committee framework.

GDP Growth.beginner: India's economy is one of the world's fastest growing, expanding by 8% in the first half of this financial year, helped by government investment, consumer spending, and a growing technology sector — but rising oil prices from the Iran conflict are a new challenge.
GDP Growth.moderate: India's real GDP grew 8% YoY in H1 FY2026, well above trend, supported by strong private consumption, fixed investment, and services exports; the Iran shock is a material headwind via higher oil import costs (widening current account), shipping disruption (basmati rice exports stranded), and potential confidence shock to business investment.
GDP Growth.expert: India's growth momentum is the most resilient among major emerging markets, with both demand-side (income tax cuts, GST rationalisation) and supply-side (infrastructure investment) drivers in place; the Iran shock tests this resilience via a terms-of-trade shock (worse by approximately 0.8-1.0% of GDP at $90+ oil), a current account shock, and a financial conditions shock (RBI constrained from cutting, potential rupee pressure).

Inflation (CPI).beginner: India's prices have been rising at around 4-5%, within the Reserve Bank of India's target range, but surging oil prices from the Iran conflict will push up fuel costs and could affect the price of almost everything from food to transportation.
Inflation (CPI).moderate: India's CPI at ~4.5% (within RBI's 2-6% tolerance band) was on a gradual downward trend; the Iran shock adds 0.5pp+ to CPI via direct fuel price passthrough and logistics cost increases; the government faces the choice of absorbing the cost via fuel subsidies (fiscal deterioration) or passing it to consumers (CPI spike) — either way the RBI's rate-cutting space narrows.
Inflation (CPI).expert: India's inflation transmission from oil prices operates through multiple channels: direct (retail fuel prices, which the government can control via excise duty changes), indirect (logistics costs affecting all goods prices), and second-round (wage demands in energy-intensive sectors); the basmati rice export disruption could paradoxically reduce domestic rice supply pressures, but this is offset by global food price inflation from the LNG-fertiliser price link.

Unemployment.beginner: India's official unemployment figures are around 7-8%, but the reality is more complex — many people work in informal jobs not captured by official statistics, and quality employment for India's growing young population remains a persistent challenge.
Unemployment.moderate: India's labour market data quality is limited (PLFS annual survey), but high-frequency indicators suggest urban unemployment around 7-8% with significant underemployment in the informal sector; the Iran shipping disruption directly threatens employment in the basmati rice export supply chain (farmers, traders, port workers) — a sector employing millions in Punjab and Haryana.
Unemployment.expert: India's employment challenge is fundamentally one of creating sufficient formal sector jobs for a labour force growing by 8-10 million annually; the manufacturing sector has not generated the required job growth, and services sector AI-driven productivity increases are reducing employment intensity in IT; the Iran shock's impact on oil-dependent logistics and informal sector real incomes adds a cyclical headwind to a structural employment gap.

Budget Deficit.beginner: India's government spends considerably more than it collects in taxes, with a deficit of around 4.5-5% of GDP, and higher oil prices could force the government to increase fuel subsidies — adding further to the borrowing requirement.
Budget Deficit.moderate: India's fiscal deficit (central government ~4.5% of GDP) faces upside risk from the Iran oil shock: the government can absorb oil price increases via strategic excise duty reductions (historically the tool used), but this would widen the fiscal deficit; alternatively, pass-through to consumers risks political backlash and direct CPI impact.
Budget Deficit.expert: India's fuel subsidy architecture has been partially reformed but the political economy of energy prices creates fiscal risk: at $90+ oil, the government is likely to reduce excise duties (₹8-13 per litre cut could cost ₹1.0-1.5tn annually, or 0.3-0.5% of GDP), worsening the fiscal deficit and potentially delaying the consolidation path that rating agencies (Moody's Baa3, S&P BBB-) are monitoring for a potential upgrade.

Current Account.beginner: India buys more from the rest of the world than it sells, mainly because it must import large amounts of oil and coal for its energy needs — and when oil prices surge as they have this week, India's trade gap widens significantly.
Current Account.moderate: India's current account deficit is set to widen materially from the Iran oil shock: oil is ~25-28% of India's import bill, and a 25-36% oil price increase adds $20-30bn annually to import costs; simultaneously, the basmati rice export disruption reduces a key export revenue stream, creating a twin shock to the goods trade balance.
Current Account.expert: India's current account, which had been narrowing toward 1.5% of GDP on services export strength and Gulf remittances, faces a structural reversal: higher oil costs (wider goods deficit), reduced rice exports, and potentially reduced Gulf remittances if Gulf economies contract — a triple-channel deterioration that could push the current account deficit above 3% of GDP, triggering RBI FX intervention and constraining monetary easing.

Policy Rate.beginner: India's central bank has been cutting interest rates to support strong economic growth, but the jump in oil prices from the Iran conflict could force it to pause or reverse these cuts to prevent inflation from rising too fast.
Policy Rate.moderate: The RBI has been on an easing trajectory; the Iran oil shock creates a classic external shock dilemma — higher inflation argues for holding, weaker growth outlook (oil cost drag) argues for cutting; the duration of the Hormuz closure will determine which consideration dominates the RBI's decision at its next meeting.
Policy Rate.expert: The RBI's monetary policy framework (flexible inflation targeting, 4% CPI target, 2-6% band) should theoretically allow it to look through supply-shock inflation if temporary; however, India's experience with persistent fuel inflation passthrough and the political sensitivity of CPI during election cycles suggest the RBI will be cautious about cutting into an energy price spike — effectively pausing the easing cycle for at least one to two quarters.

beginner: South Africa's economy is barely growing at 1.5%, meaning the country is not creating enough jobs or wealth to improve most people's lives.
This slowdown matters because unemployment already sits at 32.5%, so weak growth leaves millions with no path to employment.
Watch whether energy blackouts ease, because power cuts are strangling manufacturing and forcing businesses to relocate.
moderate: At 1.5%, South Africa's growth trails Nigeria (3.2%) and Egypt (2.8%), signaling that structural issues, not just global headwinds, are the constraint.
The energy crisis is the primary culprit, with state utility Eskom still unable to meet peak demand despite maintenance improvements in 2025.
Recovery hinges on private investment in renewables and grid modernization, neither of which moves at the speed the labor market requires.
expert: 1.5% growth combined with 32.5% unemployment and a 4.8% budget deficit reveals a productivity trap, where fiscal drag and capital underutilization reinforce stagnation.
The yield curve at +151bps and 10Y bonds yielding 8.26% price in structural risk, not cyclical recovery, meaning markets expect subdued potential growth.
Watch 2026 Q2 power generation data and private capital formation in the renewable energy sector, the binding constraints on acceleration above 2%.

beginner: Inflation at 3.5% means prices are barely rising, which sounds good but masks the real problem: people cannot find jobs to earn the money to pay those stable prices.
The South African Reserve Bank kept rates at 6.25% because inflation stayed under control, not because the economy is thriving.
If energy costs spike due to rand weakness, inflation could jump fast, forcing the central bank to tighten when growth is already fragile.
moderate: At 3.5%, inflation sits near the SARB's 4.5% midpoint target, but this reflects weak domestic demand and subdued wage growth, not monetary victory.
The rand weakened to 17.10 per USD in March 2026, yet import price pass-through has been muted because domestic absorption is so low.
The 151bps yield curve steepness signals market expectations for either a rate cut or a growth shock, not sustained stability at current policy levels.
expert: CPI at 3.5% with unemployment at 32.5% and growth at 1.5% reflects severe demand destruction, not price anchor credibility.
Core inflation momentum and goods import price indices (especially energy) will determine whether the SARB can deliver a 50bps cut in Q2 2026 without sacrificing rand stability.
The 8.26% 10Y yield pricing in a 175bps risk premium over USTs implies markets expect either inflation reacceleration or currency depreciation if policy eases below 6.0%.

beginner: One in three South Africans cannot find a job, and this rate has barely budged despite the central bank holding rates steady.
Young people face the worst of it, with youth unemployment often double the headline rate, creating a lost generation disconnected from the workforce.
Without GDP growth accelerating fast, this number will stay stuck because employers have no reason to hire when demand is flat.
moderate: At 32.5%, South Africa's unemployment is among the worst globally, worse than Brazil (8%) or Mexico (2.8%), a structural labor market failure, not a cyclical downturn.
Skills mismatch and spatial disconnection (jobs in cities, workers in townships) explain why growth and hiring do not correlate, a problem no rate cut solves alone.
Government wage bill constraints and education quality deterioration mean public sector job creation and skills pipelines are both shrinking, trapping unemployment structurally high.
expert: 32.5% unemployment with NEET (not in education, employment, or training) rates above 40% for ages 15-24 signal permanent labor force exit, not cyclical joblessness.
Quarterly data from late 2025 showed formalization declining and informal sector absorption plateauing, meaning marginal job creation is disappearing even in low-productivity segments.
Watch sectoral hiring in renewable energy and telecommunications infrastructure, the only domestic sources of job creation not dependent on commodity exports or import substitution.

beginner: The government spends 4.8% more than it takes in each year, meaning it is borrowing money to cover the gap instead of fixing the problem.
This deficit is why bond yields are so high at 8.26%, because lenders demand extra return for the risk that debt spirals.
If the deficit keeps widening, South Africa could lose its investment-grade rating, making borrowing even more expensive and crowding out private investment.
moderate: At 4.8% of GDP, the deficit exceeded the National Treasury's revised 2026 target by 0.3 percentage points, driven by wage bill pressures and lower tax revenue from weak growth.

The debt-to-GDP ratio reached 73% in 2025, above the level Moody's flagged as a downgrade risk, and deficit reduction now requires either revenue increases or spending cuts that are politically toxic.
The 10Y yield at 8.26% versus 10Y US Treasuries at 3.8% reflects both default risk and fiscal sustainability concerns, not just inflation risk.
expert: The 4.8% deficit with 1.5% growth and 3.5% inflation means the fiscal impulse is expansionary in real terms, yet unemployment sits at 32.5%, signaling that public spending is poorly allocated to growth constraints (energy, skills, infrastructure quality).
Debt service costs consumed 15.2% of tax revenue by Q4 2025, crowding out education and maintenance spending and reducing the deficit's multiplier effect below 0.8.
Watch 2026 medium-term budget policy statement revisions in late Q2, where the Treasury must either announce credible consolidation (risking recession) or face a ratings downgrade within 6 months.

beginner: South Africa sends out more money than it brings in from exports, running a deficit of 1.4% of GDP, which means the country depends on foreign borrowing to balance the books.
This deficit shows that South Africans import more goods than they export, a sign that local industries cannot compete or produce what the economy needs.
If foreign investors lose confidence, they pull their money out, and the rand falls fast, making imports expensive and inflation jump.
moderate: At 1.4% of GDP, the current account deficit narrowed from 2.1% in 2024 due to lower oil imports and subdued demand, not export strength.
Mining exports remain 44% of total exports, leaving South Africa exposed to commodity price swings, while manufacturing export share has contracted to 26% due to energy costs and labor rigidities.
The rand at 17.10 per USD reflects the combination of current account weakness and carry-trade unwinding, not fundamentals, and volatility will persist as long as the deficit persists.
expert: The 1.4% current account deficit with a 151bps yield curve steepness and 8.26% 10Y yields signals that foreign capital inflows are barely covering the gap, creating currency vulnerability at 17.10 ZAR/USD.
Q4 2025 data showed mining exports flat year-over-year while import cover fell to 4.6 months, below the 5.5 month comfort level, constraining policy space for currency flexibility.

Watch the composition of capital inflows in Q1 2026, specifically foreign direct investment versus hot money flows, because foreign reserve adequacy and debt refinancing risk hinge on whether the deficit is financed by equity or debt.

beginner: The central bank charges 6.25% interest, keeping borrowing expensive for businesses and homebuyers, because it is worried about inflation and currency weakness.
This high rate slows the economy down, which is why growth is stuck at 1.5%, but the bank cannot cut rates much without risking the rand falling further.
If unemployment stays at 32.5%, eventually political pressure will force the bank to cut, even if it means the rand tumbles and imports get pricier.
moderate: At 6.25%, the SARB's real policy rate sits at 2.75% (nominal rate minus 3.5% inflation), restrictive compared to the Fed's 4.75%, yet growth remains anemic because the economy's constraints are not monetary.
The bank held steady in March 2026 despite inflation hitting its comfort zone, signaling concern about rand depreciation and foreign capital flows more than price stability.
Market pricing shows 50bps of cuts by year-end 2026, but only if the rand stabilizes above 17.50 and inflation expectations remain anchored below 4.0%.
expert: The 6.25% policy rate paired with 8.26% 10Y yields and a 1.5% growth rate creates a classic policy bind, where raising rates to defend the currency chokes growth further, and cutting risks a depreciation spiral.

The SARB's reaction function shifted toward currency stability in late 2025, holding steady even as inflation dipped to 3.5%, suggesting the implicit carry-trade target is 6.0-6.25%, not monetary conditions.

Forward guidance and Q1 2026 MPC minutes point to a 25bps cut in May conditional on ZAR/USD staying below 17.50, but watch USD/emerging-market flows post-Fed meetings, which now dominate SARB signaling.

beginner: South Africa's stock market fell 3.7% so far in 2026, meaning investors are pulling money out because they do not believe the economy will grow.
The biggest companies on the market are mining and banks, and both are struggling because commodity prices are weak and unemployment means fewer loans get repaid.
Until growth picks up or energy gets cheaper, the market will stay under pressure because profits depend on economic activity that is not happening.
moderate: The 3.7% YTD decline masks divergence, with banking stocks down 7.2% (due to credit stress from unemployment) and defensive consumer staples flat, as foreigners reduce exposure to emerging-market currency risk.
Foreign investors net-sold ZAR 12.4 billion of equities in Q1 2026, accelerating the outflow pattern from 2025, driven by carry-trade unwinding and higher US real rates.
The JSE's dividend yield at 5.8% attracts some value hunters, but only if the rand stabilizes and earnings do not disappoint, a risky bet with 1.5% growth.
expert: The 3.7% ZAR decline and 2.5% USD decline YTD represent currency drag offsetting a 1.2% ZAR-denominated price index gain, signaling that the market repriced emerging-market risk premium upward 120bps over the past 6 months.
Earnings revisions for 2026 turned negative in February 2026 for the first time since late 2024, with consensus EPS growth now at -1.3%, driven by mining downgrades and banking provisions.

Watch Q1 earnings season (April/May 2026) for capital allocation signals, specifically whether firms accelerate share buybacks or dividend cuts, which will determine whether the 5.8% yield is sustainable or a value trap.

beginner: South Africa's 10-year government bonds yield 8.26%, meaning lenders demand a lot of extra return to lend money to the country for a decade.
This high yield reflects two fears: inflation might rise again, and the government might not be able to repay its debts.
If yields keep climbing, the government's interest payments will explode, forcing it to cut other spending and making the deficit problem worse.
moderate: At 8.26%, the 10Y yield is 440bps above the US 10Y (3.8%), a spread that widened 60bps since January 2026 as foreign investors exited emerging-market debt on Fed-tightening fears.

The spread exceeds historical averages despite inflation at 3.5% versus US inflation at 2.2%, signaling that the market prices fiscal sustainability risk (4.8% deficit, 73% debt-to-GDP) as the binding constraint.

The 151bps yield curve steepness shows investors are demanding premium compensation for duration risk, betting that either the SARB cuts rates aggressively in 2027 or the currency depreciates further.
expert: The 8.26% 10Y yield implies a 5.26% real yield after 3.5% inflation, the highest since mid-2023, and the 440bps spread to USTs reflects a cumulative default risk premium of 280bps (after stripping out term premium), pricing in a 5-year average default probability above 3.2%.

The February 2026 long-end sell-off (10Y up 22bps in one month) was driven by foreign institutional deleveraging and collateral stress, not by domestic inflation expectations, shown by 2Y yields moving only 8bps.

Fiscal sustainability hinges on whether the Treasury can achieve 1.5pp of consolidation by 2027 without triggering recession, a probability the market assesses at <40%, making further yield curve steepening likely if growth disappoints in Q2.

beginner: The curve between short-term and long-term bond yields is steep at 151 basis points, meaning lenders think the country is risky and demand much more interest to lend for longer periods.
A steep curve usually means investors expect either rates to fall later, or trouble coming soon, so they demand extra cushion for waiting.
If the curve flattens back to normal, it would mean the crisis fears are fading, but right now the steep curve is a warning sign.
moderate: At 151bps, the curve steepness (10Y minus 2Y) sits at the 90th percentile of the past decade, steeper than it was in the 2020 pandemic panic, signaling heightened tail risk perception.
The steepness reflects not growth expectations but rather currency depreciation and external financing risk, because forward guidance shows the SARB will not cut aggressively until 2027 at earliest.

Historically, curves this steep have preceded either a policy crisis (rating downgrade, currency attack) or a sharp growth shock, making term premium compression a key watch indicator for the next six months.
expert: The 151bps curve steepness with a 2Y yield at 6.75% and 10Y at 8.26% reflects two distinct factors: the 2Y prices near-term policy hold at 6.25%, while the 10Y embeds a 75bps net depreciation path (carry unwind) and 2pp of cumulative fiscal deterioration by 2030.
OIS markets price only 25bps of cuts over 12 months, yet the curve carries a 175bps term premium (historical average is 80bps), indicating skewed tail risk in credit markets, not growth optimism.

Watch the 5Y5Y inflation expectation (derived from bond yields), currently at 3.8%, which must remain above 3.5% to avoid curve inversion signals, a critical technical threshold for policy guidance in May 2026.

beginner: The rand trades at 17.10 per dollar, meaning it takes 17.10 rands to buy one dollar, and this is a weaker level than a year ago when it was 16.50.
A weaker rand makes imports more expensive, so food, fuel, and medicine costs will rise if this trend continues, hurting people who already struggle with unemployment.
If the rand falls much further, the central bank might have to raise rates to defend it, which would choke growth even more.
moderate: At 17.10, the rand has depreciated 3.6% year-to-date, tracking broader emerging-market weakness (Mexican peso, Brazilian real, Indian rupee all down 2-4%), but the ZAR underperformed due to the 1.4% current account deficit and policy uncertainty.

Carry-trade unwinding and foreign institutional deleveraging accounted for 60% of the depreciation pressure, with commodity price softness and energy crisis headlines creating a secondary bid for dollars.
The 151bps steep yield curve shows the market priced in further 3-5% depreciation by end-2026, as the SARB cannot defend currency without losing growth headroom, a trilemma with no good exit.
expert: The 17.10 level sits 4.3% weaker than the January 2026 high of 16.35, driven by 65% carry-trade liquidation (estimated ZAR 18bn outflows in Q1 2026) and 35% macro rebalancing (asset managers reducing emerging-market equity allocations).

Forward implied depreciation to 17.85 by December 2026 (priced in 3-month forwards at 17.42) reflects a consensus that political pressure forces a 50bps cut in H2 2026, weakening real rates by 100bps, with no offsetting terms-of-trade improvement.

The critical support level is 17.50, where USD funding stress (carry-trade margin calls) peaks, and a break below 17.00 would require either a 200bps risk-off repricing or a surprise SARB hike, making March-May currency dynamics a leading indicator for policy risk.

beginner: If you invest in South African stocks using US dollars, you are down 2.5% in 2026, which is worse than just holding dollars, because the rand weakness is eating away at your gains.
This matters because foreign investors, who own about 40% of the JSE, are losing money on currency, so they are pulling out faster than local buyers can absorb the shares.
Until the rand stabilizes or stocks start making bigger profits, foreign money will keep leaving, pushing prices down.
moderate: The 2.5% USD return versus 3.7% ZAR return reflects 1.2pp of currency headwind, showing that the market actually gained in rands but lost in hard currency, a sign of capital flight.
Foreign investors' cumulative net outflows reached ZAR 22.8bn in Q1 2026, the largest quarterly exit since COVID 2020, driven by both emerging-market rotation and South Africa specific fiscal fears.

The 5.8% dividend yield on the JSE is attractive in USD terms only if the rand stabilizes, but with 1.4% current account deficit and political uncertainty, the carry risk is asymmetric to the downside.
expert: The 2.5% USD decline versus 3.7% ZAR decline (currency drag of 1.2pp) masks that the equity price index in ZAR terms gained only 1.2%, meaning the market repriced downward 2.5pp in real terms, with earnings revisions at 1.3pp decline and multiple expansion of 1.2pp.

Foreign portfolio flows (tracked via TIC data and JSE foreign participation) show a -22.8bn ZAR institutional net outflow, with buy-side asset managers (ETF rebalancers and hedge funds) accounting for 75% of the selling, signaling technical flows, not fundamental value discovery.

Watch April 2026 foreign participation flows post-Fed meeting and Q1 earnings reports, because if either the SARB signals a cut or earnings stabilize, foreign technical selling could reverse 200-300bps of the current USD drawdown.

beginner: South Africa's inflation at 3.49% is right where the central bank wants it, which means the rate cutting cycle can continue without fear of losing control.
Growth is finally picking up as energy and infrastructure reforms start to work. The economy is expected to accelerate from 1.0% last year to 1.2% this year, a small but real shift.
The problem is unemployment at 32.5%, one of the world's highest. Even with reforms working, the economy is not growing fast enough to create jobs at the pace the country needs.
moderate: CPI at 3.49% sits comfortably within the South African Reserve Bank's 3-6% target band, validating the rate cut path. The 6.75% policy rate leaves room for another 50 basis points of easing before the SARB hits neutral, signaling confidence that disinflation is entrenched.

Infrastructure and energy reforms have begun lifting growth expectations, but 1.2% is still anemic by emerging market standards. Load shedding intensity has fallen from crisis peaks, allowing manufacturing to stabilize, but the growth impulse remains fragile and dependent on continued reform execution.

The unemployment rate at 32.5% is the binding constraint on policy and explains why the SARB will cut despite a 1.4% current account deficit. Without job creation, the social and political tolerance for orthodox monetary policy erodes, making the central bank's easing cycle a bet on reforms delivering a growth acceleration that shifts aggregate demand and labor demand together.
expert: CPI at 3.49% versus 3.5% full-year forecast tracking very tight, and core inflation subdued, freeing the SARB to cut. At 6.75% the policy rate is still 75 basis points above estimated neutral, suggesting 3-4 cuts remain in the cycle unless electricity or import price shocks materialize.

Growth acceleration from 1.0% to 1.2% is modest but directionally meaningful if sustained. Load shedding has declined from 6,000+ MWh per day to under 2,000 MWh as new renewable capacity came online, removing the main drag on manufacturing utilization and productivity. Monitor Q1 factory output as a leading signal of whether this reform benefit persists.

32.5% unemployment against 1.2% growth creates a policy trap. Even if the SARB cuts rates to stimulate demand, GDP growth must accelerate toward 3-4% to absorb new labor force entrants and bring unemployment down meaningfully. If reforms stall and growth stays stuck below 2%, political pressure for fiscal expansion will force central bank accommodation, risking a renewed inflation cycle.

fxRegime.label: Free Float
fxRegime.beginner: South Africa's rand floats freely — its value is determined by markets. The South African Reserve Bank (SARB) does not target a specific exchange rate, though it may intervene to smooth extreme volatility. USD/ZAR shows how many rand you need to buy one US dollar. At 17.8, one dollar costs about 18 rand. The rand is volatile because South Africa depends on commodity exports and foreign capital inflows — when global investors get nervous, the rand often falls sharply.
fxRegime.moderate: Free float. The SARB does not target an exchange rate level but has intervened in the past to rebuild reserves and smooth disorderly moves. The rand is one of the most liquid EM currencies, heavily traded as a proxy for EM risk. Key drivers: commodity prices (gold, platinum, coal), risk appetite (high beta to global sentiment), and the US-SA rate differential supporting carry trades.
fxRegime.expert: Free float with no systematic intervention since the mid-2000s reserve accumulation program. ZAR is the most liquid African currency and trades as a high-beta EM proxy — correlation with VIX typically >0.6 in stress. Carry attractiveness (repo-Fed funds spread ~325bp) supports portfolio inflows but creates vulnerability to sudden stops. Forward points reflect the wide rate differential. SARB's FX reserve position (~$55bn) provides moderate import cover (~5 months) but is below the Guidotti rule threshold when including short-term external debt.

GDP Growth.beginner: South Africa's economy is slowly recovering after years of electricity blackouts, with power supplies now more reliable, but the country still faces high unemployment, weak consumer spending, and now rising fuel prices from the Iran conflict.
GDP Growth.moderate: South Africa's GDP growth is forecast at ~1.5-2.0% for 2026, supported by the end of load-shedding and a gold price windfall; the Iran shock is a mixed signal — higher gold and platinum prices improve mining revenues, but higher fuel costs add to household and business costs in an already infrastructure-constrained economy.
GDP Growth.expert: South Africa's growth trajectory post-load-shedding represents a meaningful positive supply-side shock, but the economy's recovery potential is constrained by structural factors: rail and port logistics remain severely impaired (Transnet's operational problems), labour market rigidities limit sectoral reallocation, and the fiscal position is too tight to deploy meaningful countercyclical stimulus.

Inflation (CPI).beginner: South African prices have been rising at around 4-5%, within the central bank's target range, but higher oil prices will push up fuel costs and transport prices, potentially taking inflation toward the upper end of the target or beyond.
Inflation (CPI).moderate: SARB CPI target is 3-6%; the Iran oil shock is a direct upside risk via fuel price passthrough (petrol and diesel are partially regulated in South Africa), and a weaker rand during risk-off episodes amplifies imported inflation; SARB may pause its rate-cutting cycle or reduce the pace of cuts in response.
Inflation (CPI).expert: South Africa's inflation dynamics are uniquely sensitive to the ZAR/USD exchange rate: a 10% rand depreciation (common during EM risk-off episodes) adds approximately 1.0-1.5pp to CPI via imported goods and energy price passthrough; the Iran-driven risk-off environment creates dual inflationary pressure — higher USD-denominated oil prices AND a weaker rand that amplifies the domestic price impact.

Unemployment.beginner: South Africa has one of the highest unemployment rates in the world, with around 32-33% of people unable to find work by the narrow definition — a deep structural problem that economic cycles alone cannot solve.
Unemployment.moderate: South Africa's unemployment (32.5% narrow, 42%+ expanded) reflects decades of structural under-investment, skills mismatch, and labour market rigidities that commodity price cycles do not address; the gold price windfall improves formal mining employment but the broader labour market challenge requires skills development and industrial policy reforms beyond the capacity of any single commodity cycle.
Unemployment.expert: South Africa's unemployment crisis has multiple structural roots: spatial apartheid legacy, dysfunctional basic education, labour market rigidities from bargaining councils that price low-skill workers out of formal employment, and infrastructure collapse that has driven deindustrialisation; the Iran gold windfall generates fiscal revenue but cannot structurally address these embedded constraints without sustained multi-year institutional reform.

Budget Deficit.beginner: South Africa's government is spending more than it collects, with a deficit of around 4-5% of GDP, and high interest payments on its large debt take up a growing share of the budget — though gold price revenues from mining taxes could provide some relief.
Budget Deficit.moderate: South Africa's fiscal deficit (~4-5% of GDP) is under structural pressure from a high debt interest burden (nearly 20% of expenditure); the gold price windfall (above $5,100/oz) provides incremental royalty and corporate tax revenue that modestly improves the fiscal outlook — a rare positive amid a challenging consolidation path.
Budget Deficit.expert: South Africa's debt trajectory (approaching 75% of GDP) has been the primary concern of Moody's (Ba2 subinvestment grade); the gold and PGM price surge from the Iran shock provides a temporary positive fiscal impulse (mining royalties are formula-based on revenue), but structural spending pressures (social wages, Eskom and Transnet bailouts, public sector wages) make a durable fiscal improvement difficult without the kind of conditionality that is politically untenable.

Current Account.beginner: South Africa generally earns more from selling its minerals and gold overseas than it spends on imports — and with gold prices surging, the country's trade position is improving, even as fuel import costs rise.
Current Account.moderate: South Africa's current account is improving mechanically from the gold price surge ($5,100/oz), partially offset by higher fuel import costs and Transnet rail constraints that limit the volume of mineral exports that can physically reach ports.
Current Account.expert: South Africa's trade account under the Iran shock reflects competing forces: gold and PGM export revenues surge (positive), fuel import costs rise (negative), and Transnet port/rail limitations cap the volume uplift from higher commodity prices; the capital account remains the dominant BOP driver, with ZAR direction determined primarily by global EM risk appetite — creating net BOP uncertainty that limits SARB easing optionality.

Policy Rate.beginner: South Africa's central bank has been slowly cutting interest rates as inflation has fallen toward target, but higher fuel prices from the oil spike could force it to slow this process to prevent inflation from rising above the upper end of its 3-6% target range.
Policy Rate.moderate: SARB has been cutting rates from 2023-24 highs, with inflation tracking toward the 4.5% midpoint; the Iran shock's dual impact (higher fuel CPI + weaker ZAR) argues for pausing cuts at the next MPC meeting, as the combined inflationary impulse could push CPI toward the upper 6% boundary — historically the trigger for SARB hawkishness.
Policy Rate.expert: The SARB's reaction function is asymmetric relative to EM peers: given South Africa's investment-grade aspiration and the rand's structural volatility, the SARB tends to hold rates higher for longer than fundamentals alone would warrant to maintain the ZAR's attractiveness to carry traders; the Iran shock's ZAR depreciation pressure effectively tightens financial conditions regardless of the official rate, suggesting the SARB may hold rates and allow ZAR adjustment to do the work — a passive monetary tightening via currency channel.

beginner: Brazil's economy grew just 1.7% last year, which is slower than most big countries and means fewer new jobs and less money flowing around.
That 1.7% growth comes while tariffs are shrinking Brazil's exports, so the real challenge is that the economy isn't expanding fast enough to offset trade damage.
Compare this to the 2.9% growth Brazil averaged in the 2010s, and you see how much weaker momentum has become, raising questions about whether structural reforms can unlock faster expansion.
moderate: At 1.7%, Brazil underperforms Mexico's 2.3% and the global median of 2.1%, a gap that widens when tariff headwinds hit manufacturing-dependent exporters hardest.

The central bank holds policy rates at 12% to combat inflation, which starves growth by making borrowing expensive, creating a bind where fighting inflation suppresses the very expansion needed to improve fiscal metrics.
Capital inflows to Brazilian equities (up 13.1% YTD in local currency) contradict weak GDP, signaling that investors bet on mean reversion rather than believing current growth rates are sustainable.
expert: Brazil's 1.7% growth sits 110bps below its 2010-2019 trend, while real policy rates of 7.8% (12% nominal minus 4.2% inflation) remain restrictive enough to suppress fixed investment, the key lever for structural acceleration.

The inverted yield curve (minus 140bps) embedded in current data signals market skepticism about the central bank's willingness to ease before inflation reaches 3%, creating a growth recession risk if rate cuts delay beyond Q3 2026.

Watch the next two quarterly GDP prints for signs of manufacturing stabilization (tariff pass-through timing) versus consumption weakness (labor market stress at 6.5% unemployment), as the trajectory splits between soft landing and contraction.

beginner: Brazil's inflation at 4.2% sits above the central bank's 3% target, meaning the purchasing power of wages keeps eroding and the central bank has no reason to cut interest rates yet.
Energy prices pushed by global pressures are the main culprit here, not runaway domestic demand, which is why the central bank can't easily solve this problem by stimulating the economy.
With inflation still above target, anyone holding cash loses value, and borrowers face higher mortgage and credit card rates, which slows spending and hiring.
moderate: At 4.2%, Brazil's inflation remains 120bps above the 3% target midpoint and 40bps above the 3.75% ceiling, keeping the central bank in tightening mode despite growth stalling at 1.7%.

Global energy shocks account for much of the overshoot, but Brazil's 6.7% fiscal deficit (among the largest for emerging markets) means the government pumps money into the economy just as the central bank tries to drain it, forcing rates to stay higher longer.

The real policy rate of 7.8% is the highest in emerging markets right now, which explains why the real appreciates against the dollar even as tariff risk mounts, a disconnect unsustainable if inflation falls faster than expected.
expert: CPI at 4.2% has risen 30bps in the past month alone, driven by food and fuel pass-through that suggests the central bank's 12% policy rate is not yet terminal, with market pricing implying no cuts until late Q2 2026.

The fiscal deficit of 6.7% of GDP creates persistent demand-side inflation pressure that monetary policy alone cannot offset, meaning real rates must stay punitive (7.8% real) to clear the market without triggering currency collapse or debt dynamics instability.

Watch for the next IPCA print in early April to confirm whether the 4.2% figure marks peak inflation or a plateau, as any slip back above 4.5% forces the central bank to signal hawkish hold language through mid-year, extending growth suppression.

beginner: At 6.5%, Brazil's unemployment rate means roughly 1 in 15 people looking for work can't find a job, which is low enough to support wage growth but high enough to show the economy isn't creating jobs fast enough.
The 1.7% growth rate is too slow to absorb new entrants into the labor market, so the unemployment rate could tick up if growth doesn't accelerate in the next two quarters.
Workers with jobs feel secure enough that they can demand higher wages, which pushes inflation higher and forces the central bank to keep rates high, creating a vicious cycle.
moderate: At 6.5%, Brazil's unemployment sits below the 2022 peak of 11.9% but above the pre-pandemic 2019 level of 6.2%, revealing that job growth has barely kept pace with population growth rather than producing genuine labor market slack.

Wage growth has accelerated to 5% year-over-year despite 1.7% GDP growth, a divergence that signals workers are shifting from precarious to formal employment rather than broad productivity gains, unsustainable if growth remains sluggish.

Underemployment (workers in part-time or informal roles unwillingly) sits near 7%, meaning real joblessness for policy purposes exceeds the 6.5% headline, a gap that narrows only if manufacturing rehires post-tariff adjustment.
